create-a-world.title: Create a world
create-a-world.description: A world is the place where your 3D scene lives. One call creates it, and it draws into a canvas on your page.
steps: Get the engine. It is not on npm yet: clone the repository, run pnpm install and pnpm run build in it, then add it to your project from that folder.
Put a <canvas> in your page. A canvas is a rectangle of the page that a program can draw into. Give it a width and a height.
Call createWorld with the canvas id. You get a world: a scene (the list of things to draw), a camera (the eye that looks at them) and everything that draws the picture.
Add one cube and one light, so there is something to see. The next chapters explain these lines one by one.
When your page closes, call world.dispose() to give the memory back.
create-a-world.tryIt: Drag the picture to turn around the cube. Pick another colour in the panel.

add-a-shape.title: Add a shape
add-a-shape.description: Everything you see is a mesh: a shape with a material on it. Make the shape with `geometry`, wrap it in a mesh with `object.mesh`, and add it to the scene.
steps: A shape, or geometry, is only the form: its corners and its faces. geometry.box(1, 1, 1) is a cube one metre wide, geometry.sphere(0.75) a ball. There are also cylinders, cones, rings, tori and more.
A mesh is a shape plus a material: object.mesh(shape, material). The material is the next chapter.
Place a mesh with position, turn it with rotation and size it with scale. Rotations are in radians: a full turn is Math.PI * 2.
object.group() holds several meshes, so they move together, like the plate of the turntable.
Nothing shows until you call world.scene.add(mesh).
add-a-shape.tryIt: Change the colour of the shapes, stop the spin, or turn it faster.

give-it-a-material.title: Give it a material
give-it-a-material.description: A material says what a surface is made of: its colour, whether it is metal, how rough it is. `material.meshStandard` covers almost everything.
steps: color is the paint, written like a web colour: '#e8a25a'.
metalness goes from 0 (plastic, clay, wood) to 1 (metal). A metal shows the colours of what it reflects.
roughness goes from 0 (smooth like a mirror, with small sharp highlights) to 1 (rough like chalk, with soft light everywhere).
Change a material whenever you like: chrome.roughness = 0.3. Every mesh that uses it changes at once.
Glass is material.meshPhysical with transmission: 1: light goes through it. ior, the index of refraction, says how much it bends light: 1.5 for window glass. See it in Glass on the table.
give-it-a-material.tryIt: Each column is more metal than the one before, and each row is rougher. Pick one colour for all of them, and make the lamps brighter.

light-it.title: Light it
light-it.description: Without a light, everything is black. Add lights with the `light` family, and let them cast shadows.
steps: light.directional is the sun: all its rays go the same way, and position says where it shines from.
light.point is a bulb: it shines all around and fades with distance. light.spot is a torch: a cone of light.
light.ambient is a soft light from everywhere. A little of it keeps the shadows from being pitch black.
Add castShadow: true and what the light hits throws a shadow.
intensity is how strong a light is, color its colour. Change them any time: sun.intensity = 1.
light-it.tryIt: Move the hour: the sun crosses the sky, turns red at dusk, and every shadow turns with it.

move-the-camera.title: Move the camera
move-the-camera.description: The camera is your eye in the world. Place it in code, then let the reader move it with `world.controls`.
steps: world.camera.position.set(x, y, z) puts the eye somewhere; world.camera.lookAt(x, y, z) turns it towards a point.
A controller turns the mouse, fingers and keyboard into camera moves. Choose it when you create the world: createWorld('view', { controls: 'orbit' }).
'orbit' circles a point: drag to turn, right-drag to slide, scroll to zoom. world.controls.target is the point it circles.

There are others: 'fly' (keys W A S D, see A fighter jet in the canyon), 'character' (run and jump, bumping into walls, see Temple parkour), 'firstPerson' (walk through everything), 'trackball', 'panZoom' for a flat map, and 'none' when your code moves the camera itself.
Switch at any time: world.controls.kind = 'fly'.
move-the-camera.tryIt: Drag to turn around the clock, scroll to look closely at the teeth of the gears.

animate.title: Animate
animate.description: To make things move, give the world a function to run before every picture, with `world.onFrame`.
steps: The world draws a new picture many times a second. Each picture is a frame. world.onFrame(fn) runs fn before each one.
fn receives delta: the seconds since the last frame. Multiply your speeds by it, and things move just as fast on a quick screen as on a slow one.
Call world.invalidate() to say “draw again”. When nothing asks for a new frame, the world rests: a scene that does not move costs nothing.

For a motion made of poses, like a walk, use the animation mixer. animation.clip lists the poses and when they happen; animation.createMixer(robot).play(clip) plays them and fills in the moments between. See Blending robot motions.
animate.tryIt: Change the height and the speed of the wave. Double-click the floor to drop a new stone.

load-a-compiled-model.title: Load a compiled model
load-a-compiled-model.description: A model made in a 3D program is compiled once, then one line adds it to your world. The engine then loads only the parts the camera needs.
steps: Most 3D programs export glTF files (.gltf or .glb), the common format for 3D models.

The compiler cuts the model into small pieces called clusters, patches of about a hundred triangles, and saves each one at several levels of detail. Run it once, in a terminal: the model, the output folder, full to keep the whole model, a triangle budget, and the web address the folder will be served from.
Put the output folder on your web server, at that address.
In the page, await world.scene.load(url) adds the model. It gives back the model, with its size in bounds, to frame the camera.
The model is never downloaded whole. The engine fetches the pieces the camera sees, finer as you come closer. This is called streaming.
load-a-compiled-model.tryIt: Turn the lamp around the head, raise it, change its colour.

stay-within-memory.title: Stay within memory
stay-within-memory.description: A big model does not have to fit in memory. You give the engine a fixed amount, and it keeps what the view needs most inside it.
steps: The GPU, the chip that draws the picture, has its own memory, and a web page cannot ask how much of it is free. So you choose the amount yourself.
world.budget.geometryPool is the memory for shapes; world.budget.texturePool is the memory for the images painted on surfaces, called textures. Both are counted in bytes.
When the view needs more than the budget, nothing breaks: far and small parts are drawn with fewer triangles until everything fits. The picture stays whole, only less detailed.
Read the value back to see what the engine really holds.
See the pieces with world.diagnostic.mode = 'clusters': each cluster gets its own colour.
stay-within-memory.tryIt: Slide the memory down: the pieces grow bigger, the building stays whole. Switch the view to clusters to see them.

make-things-fall.title: Make things fall
make-things-fall.description: Turn the physics on and your shapes gain weight: they fall, bump and come to rest.
steps: Give the world physics: true. The simulation runs apart from the drawing, in a worker, so it never slows the picture down.
Mark the floor 'static': it holds the others and never moves. Mark a box 'dynamic': gravity pulls it.
The shape comes from the geometry, the weight from the material: physics: 'wood' is light, 'metal' is heavy, 'rubber' bounces.
Push a body with applyImpulse, or listen to its contact. Once every body sleeps, nothing is computed and nothing is drawn.
A model loaded with scene.load collides with its own triangles, cooked when it was compiled. await world.raycast(point, { exact: true }) finds the very triangle under the cursor.
make-things-fall.tryIt: Drop more boxes, switch the gravity to the Moon, and turn on slow motion.

touch-and-react.title: Touch and react
touch-and-react.description: Walk into your world: with the physics on, the character climbs, rides and pushes what it meets, and what it meets pushes back.
steps: Create the world with controls: 'character' and physics: true. The character is now a body of the physics, like the boxes.
Mark what never moves 'static': the floor, the stairs, the walls. The character climbs steps up to its knee and slopes up to 45°.
Mark a platform 'kinematic' and move it from your code each frame: whatever stands on it rides along.
Make boxes 'dynamic' and light: the character pushes them with pushStrength newtons, and they fall, tumble and push back.
touch-and-react.tryIt: Click the picture, walk with W A S D, jump with Space. Climb the stairs, ride the platform, push the stack of boxes.

connect-drive-and-break.title: Connect, drive and break
connect-drive-and-break.description: Joints hold two bodies together, or a body to the world: a door turns on its hinge, a drawer slides on its rail, a chain hangs by its links, and a bridge breaks when pulled too hard.
steps: Make a joint with joint.hinge(a, b, options) or its kin — fixed, point, slider, distance, cone — and give it to world.physics.add. Put null for b to hold a body to the world.
anchor is where the bodies connect and axis the way the pin or the rail points, both in the world, read when the joint is made.
limits stop the joint: radians for a hinge, metres for a slider. A spring makes the stop soft.
A motor drives a hinge or a slider to a speed or a position. Change joint.motor at any time.
breakForce is the pull, in newtons, past which the joint snaps: joint.broken turns true and joint.on('break', …) is called.

Advanced joints tie motions together: joint.gear(a, b, { ratio }) turns two hinged wheels as one train, joint.rackAndPinion turns a wheel into a slide, joint.pulley(a, b, { over }) hangs two loads on one rope, joint.path(a, b, { path }) keeps a cart on its track, and swingTwist and sixDof make shoulders and joints of your own.

A vehicle is a body on wheels: vehicle.car(body, { wheels }), vehicle.motorcycle or vehicle.tracked, its wheels meshes placed on the body where they rest. Add it with world.physics.add and drive it with the keyboard: world.controls.vehicle = car, then world.controls.kind = 'vehicle'. Its engine, gearbox, suspension and brakes are a real machine's; car.speed, car.gear and car.rpm tell how it goes.
connect-drive-and-break.tryIt: Open the door and the drawer, then drop the stone on the bridge. Lower the bridge strength and rebuild it: it breaks under its own weight.

your-own-scene.title: Your own scene
your-own-scene.description: You now know every piece. This chapter puts them together in one small scene that you can copy and make your own.
steps: Start like chapter 1: a canvas, and createWorld with the orbit controller.
Build with shapes and materials, as in chapters 2 and 3: an island, a house, a tree and a windmill.
Light it with a sun that casts shadows (chapter 4), and move the sun with the hour.
Turn the sails in world.onFrame (chapter 6). They are four boxes in one group, so turning the group turns them all.
Open the full code, change a number, press Run: the scene is yours. Then load a model of your own (chapter 7).
your-own-scene.tryIt: Change the hour, the wind and the colour of the roof.

install.title: Install Trillion3D
install.description: Install the package, compile a model and draw it in a page: the commands, the CDN import, the supported platforms, the two server headers and the licence.
install.html:
Install

Trillion3D is not published on npm yet; the commands below work from its first release on.

You need Node.js 22.18 or newer. In your project's folder:

npm install trillion3d

This brings the engine for the browser, the Node API and the model compiler. The compiler is a native program, and npm installs only the build for your machine: macOS on Apple silicon or Intel, Linux arm64 or x64 (glibc), Windows x64. On any other machine, compiling stops with T3D-E079; the engine itself still runs in the browser.

Compile a model

The engine draws compiled models: the compiler cuts a model into small pieces that the browser streams. Put your model in public/ — glTF, GLB, OBJ, FBX or USD — then run:

npx trillion3d-compile public/model.glb public/model slice 150000 /

In order: the model, the output folder, the scope, the triangle budget, and the address at which your server shows the model's folder. The compiled model is public/model/native/slice/manifest.json.

Draw it

Save this page as public/index.html. The importmap loads the engine from a CDN: no bundler, no build step.

<!doctype html>
<canvas id="viewer" style="width: 100%; height: 90vh"></canvas>
<script type="importmap">
  { "imports": { "trillion3d": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/trillion3d/dist/trillion3d.module.js" } }
</script>
<script type="module">
  import { createWorld, light } from 'trillion3d';

  const world = createWorld('viewer');
  world.scene.add(light.directional({ intensity: 3, position: [5, 10, 2] }));
  world.scene.add(light.ambient({ intensity: 0.4 }));
  world.camera.position.set(3, 2, 4);
  world.camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0);
  await world.scene.load('/model/native/slice/manifest.json');
</script>

Serve the public/ folder with any static web server and open its address; a page opened as a file does not work. With a bundler, import trillion3d as installed instead: the SDK guide says which files to serve beside it.

Two server headers for physics

Physics runs on several threads only in a cross-origin isolated page. Have your server send these two headers with the page:

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless

Without them everything still works: physics runs on one thread, slower with many bodies, with no error and no warning. Type crossOriginIsolated in the browser console to see which one you have. A browser that does not know credentialless needs require-corp, which asks every file from another site for a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header.

Warnings and errors

Every message of the compiler has a code and says its cause and what to do. T3D-E… is an error: nothing is written. T3D-W… is a warning: the model is compiled all the same, and --strict turns it into a failure. T3D-I… is an information, shown with --verbose.

Licence

Trillion3D is under the PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 licence. It is free for any non-commercial use: learning, personal projects, research, teaching, a charity. A commercial use needs a licence from the owner, Alban Pasquelin: ask him by opening an issue.

hlod.title: Draw far away with HLOD
hlod.description: Past the loading range, the compiler's stand-ins draw each cell of objects: four levels, from the objects batched to one simple shell per wide cell. Mark the objects, compile, draw, and check in the HLOD and triangles views.
hlod.html:
What HLOD is

A city seen from a tower holds thousands of objects past the loading range. Drawing each of them costs too many draws and too much memory; leaving them out leaves holes on the horizon. HLOD — hierarchical levels of detail — groups the objects of each cell of the ground and gives the cell stand-ins built by the compiler, each coarser and covering a wider cell than the one before. Near the camera every object is drawn itself; farther away its cell's stand-in is drawn in its place, and the view never stops at a distance.

The default chain has four levels:

  • HLOD 0: the cell's objects themselves, batched — the same meshes, drawn together past the main loading range.
  • HLOD 1, 2 and 3: one closed shell per cell, simplified to about a pixel at the distance it is first seen from, its materials baked into one texture. Each level's cells are twice as wide as the level before.

Everything is decided when the model is compiled: the page that draws it has nothing to set. See it in the example HLOD across a long district, two kilometres of street.

1. Mark the objects

The compiler builds an HLOD only over the objects it is told about. The simplest way is a mark on the glTF node, written by the tool or the code that makes the scene: buildings, foliage or props.

{
  "nodes": [
    { "name": "Tower 12", "mesh": 3, "extras": { "hlod": "buildings" } },
    { "name": "Oak 7", "mesh": 8, "extras": { "hlod": "foliage" } },
    { "name": "Bench 40", "mesh": 11, "extras": { "hlod": "props" } }
  ]
}
  • buildings: the main chain, all its levels.
  • foliage: a short chain of two levels with a voxel half as large, to keep the silhouettes of trees.
  • props: small objects, batched in cells of their own and absorbed by the main chain's first shell.

An object nothing names has no HLOD: it is streamed and drawn in its cell, and nothing stands for it farther away. Keep it that way for what moves — cars, doors, characters: an HLOD is for what stands still.

2. Compile with Node

import { prepare } from 'trillion3d';

await prepare('public/district.gltf', 'public/district', 'full', 150000, {
  resourceBaseUrl: '/',
  hlod: { levels: 4, quality: 'balanced' },
});

That is the whole option of the example: its objects are marked, so no group needs naming. Without marks, name the objects of each group — by a node's exact name, a regular expression on it, or a match on what the glTF carries (node, mesh, material, values of the node's extras; every field named must match):

await prepare('public/city.glb', 'public/city', 'slice', 150000, {
  resourceBaseUrl: '/',
  hlod: {
    levels: 4,         // 2 to 8, HLOD 0 included
    quality: 'high',   // 'low', 'balanced' or 'high'
    groups: {
      buildings: /^(House|Tower)/,
      foliage: { mesh: /tree/i },
      props: { node: /^(Lamp|Bench)/, extras: { kind: 'street' } },
    },
  },
});

A node's mark comes first; then the first group, in key order, that matches the object takes it. The quality sets every shell:

qualityDeviation allowedTexture side
'low'2 pixels512 texels
'balanced' (default)1 pixel1024 texels
'high'half a pixel2048 texels

The pixel is measured at the distance a shell is first seen from. levels defaults to 4.

3. Compile from the command line

npx trillion3d-compile '--hlod={"levels":4,"quality":"balanced"}' public/district.gltf public/district full 150000 /

The flag holds either form as JSON, anywhere on the line; a regular expression is written { "regex": "^Tree", "flags": "i" }:

npx trillion3d-compile '--hlod={"groups":{"foliage":{"mesh":{"regex":"tree","flags":"i"}}}}' public/city.glb public/city slice 150000 /

4. Compile many models at once

import { prepareMany } from 'trillion3d';

await prepareMany(
  [
    { source: 'public/district.gltf', cache: 'public/district', resourceBaseUrl: '/', hlod: { levels: 4 } },
    { source: 'public/forest.gltf', cache: 'public/forest', resourceBaseUrl: '/', hlod: { levels: 2, quality: 'low' } },
  ],
  { workers: 2 },
);

This site compiles its own example the same way: the option sits beside the code that writes the scene, and the list of scenes reads it.

// scripts/docs/examples/district.ts
export const DISTRICT_HLOD: HlodOptions = { levels: 4, quality: 'balanced' };

// scripts/site-caches.ts
'long-district': { ...example('long-district'), hlod: DISTRICT_HLOD },

5. Draw it

The page loads the compiled model as any other; the stand-ins come with it.

<!doctype html>
<canvas id="viewer" style="width: 100%; height: 90vh"></canvas>
<script type="importmap">
  { "imports": { "trillion3d": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/trillion3d/dist/trillion3d.module.js" } }
</script>
<script type="module">
  import { createWorld, light } from 'trillion3d';

  const world = createWorld('viewer', { controls: 'firstPerson' });
  world.camera.far = 3000;
  world.scene.add(light.directional({ intensity: 3, position: [60, 90, 40] }));
  world.scene.add(light.hemisphere({ intensity: 1.2 }));
  await world.scene.load('/district/native/full/manifest.json');
</script>

6. Check it

Choose the HLOD view (world.diagnostic.mode = 'hlod'): each pixel takes the colour of what drew it.

ColourWhat is drawn
whitethe object itself, within the main loading range
blueHLOD 0: the cell's objects, batched
yellowHLOD 1: one shell per cell
purpleHLOD 2: one shell per wider cell
cyanHLOD 3: one shell per widest cell (grey beyond, for a longer chain)

The colours alone prove nothing: switch to the triangles view ('wireframe'). Near, the triangles of every object; far away, a few large triangles per cell — simple boxes for whole blocks —, fewer at each level. The x-ray view shows every triangle submitted, hidden ones too: tick Freeze culling, then walk aside to see what was kept for the camera you left.

world.diagnostic.mode = 'hlod';      // white, blue, yellow, purple, cyan
world.diagnostic.mode = 'wireframe'; // simple shells far away
world.diagnostic.mode = 'xray';      // every triangle submitted, hidden ones too
world.diagnostic.freeze = true;      // hold the cut, then step aside

The expert form

For full control: named layers, each with its builder and the layer above it (parent), and rules that assign objects to the instanced layers. The simple form stands for exactly such a list; the two forms cannot be mixed.

hlod: {
  layers: [
    { name: 'buildings', builder: 'instanced', parent: 'city1' },
    { name: 'city1', builder: 'approximate', parent: 'city2', deviationPixels: 1 },
    { name: 'city2', builder: 'approximate', textureSize: 2048 },
    { name: 'trees', builder: 'instanced', parent: 'canopy' },
    { name: 'canopy', builder: 'approximate', accuracyPixels: 0.3 },
  ],
  assign: [{ match: { node: /^Tree/, extras: { kind: 'tree' } }, layer: 'trees' }],
  default: 'buildings',
}
  • Builders: instanced, the objects themselves (objects are assigned to these layers); approximate, one closed shell per cell, its materials baked; merge, the cell's objects merged into one mesh; proxy, the cell's objects remeshed into one closed surface.
  • Settings, in metres or in pixels, never both: accuracy or accuracyPixels the voxel, deviation or deviationPixels the deviation allowed, textureSize the texture side, a power of two from 16 to 8192.
  • Each rule, and default, names an instanced layer; the first rule that matches wins. A node's extras.hlod mark names a layer by its name here.

Pitfalls

  • No HLOD appears: the job names none, or no object is marked or matched — a job whose HLOD takes no object is refused.
  • A mark naming no group nor layer, a mark in a job without hlod, an unknown field, quality or group: the job is refused, in the words you wrote.
  • Something moves and leaves a ghost far away: it was given a group. Leave moving objects unnamed.
  • The far shells look too coarse: raise quality to 'high' rather than adding levels; more levels reach farther, not finer.

In depth: docs/COMPILER.md. The anti-aliasing options are set in the same call: Temporal anti-aliasing.

temporal-antialiasing.title: Temporal anti-aliasing
temporal-antialiasing.description: Smooth edges and steady fine detail: the level for the whole scene, who decides between the scene, the quality, the page and the editor, and how much history each material may keep.
temporal-antialiasing.html:
What it does

A pixel samples one point of the scene: thin wires, edges and fine textures then show stairs and shimmer. The temporal anti-aliasing shifts the camera by a fraction of a pixel at every image and blends each new image into a history of the images before, moved along with the surfaces. Over a few images every pixel gathers many samples: smooth edges, steady fine detail, at the cost of one image.

It is set at two scales: for the whole scene (a level, from off to the finest), and for each material (how much history its pixels may keep). See it in Smooth edges over time and Responsive particles.

For the whole scene

The level is written in the compiled scene, so it travels with it: 'off', 'low', 'medium', 'high' or 'max', from the cheapest to the finest. true stands for the default level, false for 'off'.

import { prepare } from 'trillion3d';

await prepare('public/street.glb', 'public/street', 'full', 150000, {
  resourceBaseUrl: '/',
  temporalAntialiasing: 'high',
});
npx trillion3d-compile --temporal-antialiasing=high public/street.glb public/street full 150000 /

In a batch, each job has its own field:

{
  "jobs": [
    { "source": "public/street.glb", "cache": "public/street", "resourceBaseUrl": "/", "temporalAntialiasing": "high" },
    { "source": "public/plan.glb", "cache": "public/plan", "resourceBaseUrl": "/", "temporalAntialiasing": "off" }
  ]
}

The page can still decide, at creation or at any moment:

const world = createWorld('viewer', { temporalAntialiasing: 'medium' });
await world.scene.load('/street/native/full/manifest.json');

world.temporalAntialiasing = 'off';  // switched live, next image
world.temporalAntialiasing = true;   // back to the default level

Who decides, from the strongest to the weakest:

RankWhoHow
1the scene editorits own setting
2the pagecreateWorld(…, { temporalAntialiasing }), world.temporalAntialiasing = …
3the quality levelthe quality the world runs at
4the compiled scenetemporalAntialiasing, --temporal-antialiasing=
5the defaultnothing named

With several scenes in one world, the first scene loaded that names a level decides for the scene rank.

For each material

Each material holds one number from 0 to 1: the share of history the anti-aliasing may keep on its pixels. 1 is the full smoothing; 0 shows its pixels from the current image alone. Four presets name the usual values:

PresetHistory keptFor
'normal'1everything, by default
'responsive'0.75small fast effects: sparks, embers, blinking lights
'soft'0.5surfaces that change a lot from one image to the next: screens, animated textures
'off'0pixels that must stay exactly as drawn: text, a user interface in the scene

Any number between is allowed. Set it by material name at compile time, or in the glTF material itself:

await prepare('public/arcade.glb', 'public/arcade', 'full', 150000, {
  resourceBaseUrl: '/',
  materials: {
    'screen': { temporalAntialiasing: 'soft' },
    'score text': { temporalAntialiasing: 'off' },
    'neon': { temporalAntialiasing: 0.6 },
  },
});
npx trillion3d-compile '--materials={"screen":{"temporalAntialiasing":"soft"}}' public/arcade.glb public/arcade full 150000 /
{ "name": "score text", "extras": { "temporalAntialiasing": "off" } }

responsive is a shortcut for 0.75 — the current image then weighs exactly a quarter: see Responsive anti-aliasing. When several settings name one material, the first of this list wins:

  1. materials: { name: { temporalAntialiasing } };
  2. materials: { name: { responsive: true } };
  3. the responsive option matching its object;
  4. "extras": { "temporalAntialiasing": … } in the glTF;
  5. "extras": { "responsive": true } in the glTF;
  6. otherwise 1.

See it

The TAA history by material view (world.diagnostic.mode = 'taa-material-history') shows each pixel's material value as grey: white 1, black 0. Compare with the no temporal AA view, the raw image of the frame, and the frame difference view, which lights whatever changed since the image before — a still view that keeps lighting up shimmers.

world.diagnostic.mode = 'taa-material-history'; // white 1, black 0
world.diagnostic.mode = 'no-temporal-aa';       // the raw image of this frame
world.diagnostic.mode = 'frame-difference';     // what changed since the last image

Pitfalls

  • 'off' on a material is sharper, but its edges then follow the camera's sub-pixel shift: they may shimmer, even when nothing moves. Keep it for text and flat interfaces.
  • A trail behind a fast object with good motion — a car, a character — is not a case for a lower value: the history follows them. Lower values are for what the engine cannot follow.
  • Turning the whole scene 'off' to fix one material costs the smoothing everywhere: set that material instead.
  • A material name is matched exactly, as written in the glTF.

The same call compiles the HLOD: Draw far away with HLOD.

responsive-antialiasing.title: Responsive anti-aliasing for fast effects
responsive-antialiasing.description: On a responsive material the current image weighs exactly a quarter, so small fast effects such as sparks leave no trail. Three ways to ask for it when compiling, which one wins, and the view that shows it.
responsive-antialiasing.html:
What it does

The temporal anti-aliasing blends each new image into a history of the images before, moved along with the surfaces (Temporal anti-aliasing). It works where the engine knows how each pixel moved. A small bright spark crossing many pixels in one image, a blinking light, an effect animated in its shader: the history cannot follow them, and they leave a trail behind them or fade.

A responsive material changes one thing: on its pixels the blend takes exactly a quarter of each new image (1/4) — it keeps 0.75 of its history —, so their history catches up within a few images. Everything else keeps the full smoothing.

When to use it

  • Yes: sparks, embers, small fast particles, blinking lights — small effects that change faster than the history can follow.
  • No: ordinary objects, even fast ones — a car, a character, a turning wheel. The engine knows their motion, the history follows them, and responsive pixels would only shimmer more.

The example Responsive particles shows the difference: two swarms of sparks with the same motion; the left one is responsive, its trails short; the right one is not.

Three ways to ask for it

The flag is set when the scene is compiled; the page changes nothing. The example's left swarm uses all three, one colour each: orange (A), cyan (B), pink (C).

A — responsive: match the objects

One match, as an HLOD group names its objects: a node's exact name, a regular expression on it, or { node, mesh, material, extras }. The materials of every object it matches become responsive; a match naming material keeps only those materials.

import { prepare } from 'trillion3d';

await prepare('public/sparks.gltf', 'public/sparks', 'full', 150000, {
  resourceBaseUrl: '/',
  responsive: { material: /^spark pattern$/ },
});

Other matches:

responsive: 'Fireworks',                       // the node named exactly Fireworks
responsive: /^Spark/,                          // every node whose name starts with Spark
responsive: { mesh: /ember/i },                // every node wearing an ember mesh
responsive: { extras: { effect: 'particles' } } // every node whose extras say so

B — materials: set a material by its name

materials: {
  'spark listed': { responsive: true },
  'still listed': { responsive: false },
  'still extras': { responsive: false },
},

An explicit value, false included, that wins over the two other ways.

C — the material's own glTF extras

{ "name": "spark extras", "extras": { "responsive": true } }

Written by whoever exports the model; no compile option needed.

Which one wins

RankWayWritten
1Bmaterials: { name: { responsive } }, false included
2Aresponsive: …
3C"extras": { "responsive": true }
4—otherwise not responsive

In the example, still extras asks for it in its extras, but materials sets it to false: it stays plain. A material's own temporalAntialiasing value, when one is named, comes before all three (Temporal anti-aliasing).

From the command line, in a batch, in this site

npx trillion3d-compile '--responsive={"material":{"regex":"^spark pattern$"}}' '--materials={"spark listed":{"responsive":true}}' public/sparks.gltf public/sparks full 150000 /
{
  "jobs": [
    {
      "source": "public/sparks.gltf",
      "cache": "public/sparks",
      "resourceBaseUrl": "/",
      "responsive": { "material": { "regex": "^spark pattern$" } },
      "materials": { "spark listed": { "responsive": true } }
    }
  ]
}

Each flag holds JSON; a regular expression is written { "regex": "^spark", "flags": "i" }. This site declares its example's options beside the code that writes the sparks:

// scripts/docs/examples/sparks.ts
export const SPARKS_RESPONSIVE: ResponsiveOption = { material: /^spark pattern$/ };
export const SPARKS_MATERIALS: MaterialsOption = {
  'spark listed': { responsive: true },
  'still listed': { responsive: false },
  'still extras': { responsive: false },
};

// scripts/site-caches.ts
'particles-responsive': {
  ...example('particles-responsive'),
  responsive: SPARKS_RESPONSIVE,
  materials: SPARKS_MATERIALS,
},

Draw it

<!doctype html>
<canvas id="viewer" style="width: 100%; height: 90vh"></canvas>
<script type="importmap">
  { "imports": { "trillion3d": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/trillion3d/dist/trillion3d.module.js" } }
</script>
<script type="module">
  import { createWorld, light } from 'trillion3d';

  const world = createWorld('viewer', { controls: 'orbit', temporalAntialiasing: true });
  world.scene.add(light.directional({ intensity: 3, position: [60, 90, 40] }));
  world.scene.add(light.hemisphere({ intensity: 1.2 }));
  await world.scene.load('/sparks/native/full/manifest.json');
</script>

See it

Choose the TAA responsive view: the responsive pixels show in white. Turn the smoothing off and on again to compare the two swarms' trails; the frame difference view lights whatever changed since the image before.

world.diagnostic.mode = 'taa-responsive';   // responsive pixels in white
world.diagnostic.mode = 'frame-difference'; // what changed since the last image

Pitfalls

  • Nothing turns white: the material name in materials must be written exactly as in the glTF, and a match naming material keeps only those materials.
  • A responsive surface shimmers a little more than the others: that is the price of following fast changes. Keep it for small effects.
  • Still a trail: lower the material's own value further, 'soft' or a number (Temporal anti-aliasing).

In depth: docs/COMPILER.md.

three-migration.title: Migration from Three.js
three-migration.description: On the left a complete Three.js program, on the right the engine program that draws the same scene, section by section.

measurement-entry.title: The measurement entry point
measurement-entry.description: Where a witness or an internal session is still nameable — never through the published `trillion3d` entry.
measurement-entry.html:
A page imports trillion3d and never sees a witness or an internal session: createWorld draws with WebGPU, or is refused by name if the machine grants none. The bench and the proofs still need to name a witness — bare Three.js, THREE.LOD, the internal openMeasuredWorld session — and that is the one job of the separate measurement entry point, packages/sdk-browser/src/measurement/measurement.ts.

It re-exports everything the published entry does, plus what a host never needs: openMeasuredWorld/createMeasuredWorldJob (the internal session a world opens on itself), the pages factory webgpuPagesEngine, and measurement-only helpers such as attachParticles. None of it reaches a published world, and none of it is imported by an application.

createWorldJob.title: A world load as a cancellable job
createWorldJob.description: A world has no dedicated job wrapper of its own: `scene.load` is a plain promise, and the generic `createJob` helper turns it into a cancellable one with progress when a host needs the same job contract compilation uses.

architecture.title: How a frame is drawn
architecture.description: The path from your scene to the picture: the pieces that are kept, the pixels that are filled, the light that is added.
architecture.html:
1. Choose the pieces. Every model is made of small patches of triangles, clusters, stored at several levels of detail. Each frame, the GPU picks for each part of the model the coarsest level that still looks exact on screen.
  2. Write who is where. The chosen triangles are drawn once into a visibility buffer: for every pixel, only the number of the triangle it shows.
  3. Paint the surfaces. Then each pixel reads its triangle's material: colour, roughness, metal, normal map. Surfaces of the same kind are painted together, in one pass.
  4. Light, then smooth. Lights and shadows are added, see-through surfaces come last, and temporal antialiasing blends each frame with the ones before it, so edges stay smooth.

When nothing moves, none of this runs: the world keeps the last picture.

The whole path: docs/ENGINE.md.

occlusion-two-phase.title: Skipping what is hidden
occlusion-two-phase.description: Why a wall hides the room behind it for free: the engine does not draw what the last frame proved hidden.
occlusion-two-phase.html:
A town has thousands of objects behind the first row of houses. Drawing them would cost time for pixels nobody sees. So the engine draws in two passes:

  1. First, what was visible in the previous frame. That gives a rough picture of the depth: how far the nearest surface is at each place of the screen.
  2. Then every other piece is tested against that depth. A piece that is fully behind is skipped; the rest is drawn.

The test only skips what is surely hidden: a wrong guess costs a second test, never a missing pixel. There is nothing to set; it is always on.

In depth: docs/ENGINE.md.

cluster-format.title: How models are packed
cluster-format.description: What the compiler writes: small pages of triangles, stored compactly, each one readable on its own.
cluster-format.html:
The compiler cuts a model into clusters of at most a hundred and twenty-eight triangles, and saves each one as a page the browser can read on its own.

  • Positions, texture coordinates and normals are rounded onto fine grids. That makes a page several times smaller than plain numbers, and the rounding stays far below a pixel.
  • Each page says how far its rounding moved a point, so the engine never guesses.
  • Pages are named by their content: two models that share a piece share its page.

The exact layout is in docs/FORMAT.md.

water-pass.title: Water and glass
water-pass.description: How a see-through material bends what is behind it: the engine reads back the picture it already drew.
water-pass.html:
Water and thick glass are not drawn like paint. The engine first draws everything solid, keeps a copy of that picture, and then, for each pixel of water or glass, reads the copy a little to the side, as light bends through the surface.

  • How much it bends and what colour it takes come from the imported material: its index of refraction, its thickness and its tint.
  • The surface also reflects the sky and the lights, more at a grazing angle, as real water does.
  • One limit: a glass does not show another glass behind it.

In depth: docs/ENGINE.md.

memory-pools.title: Where memory goes
memory-pools.description: Two fixed amounts of GPU memory, one for shapes and one for textures, and what happens when a view asks for more.
memory-pools.html:
The engine keeps two pools in GPU memory: one for the pages of shapes, one for the tiles of textures. You set their size with world.budget (chapter 8); the engine never reads the machine to guess it.

  • The coarsest version of every model always stays in, so there is never a hole.
  • When a view needs more than a pool holds, the engine draws with coarser pieces until it fits: less detail, never a missing part.
  • Changing a pool while the scene runs keeps what still fits and lets go of the rest.

In depth: docs/RESIDENCY.md.

texture-compression.title: Smaller textures
texture-compression.description: Textures are cut into tiles, loaded only where the picture needs them, and compressed when that does not change the image.
texture-compression.html:
A texture is an image painted on a surface. The compiler prepares each one at every size, from full down to tiny, and cuts them into square tiles. The browser loads only the tiles the picture shows, at the size it shows them.

The compiler can also store the tiles in a compressed format the GPU reads directly, about four times smaller. It keeps the compressed version only when it looks the same as the original; otherwise the tile stays uncompressed. A tile that has not arrived yet shows a smaller version of itself, never a hole.

In depth: docs/RESIDENCY.md.

shadow-pages.title: Shadows in pieces
shadow-pages.description: Why a moving camera redraws only a strip of its shadows: the shadow map is cut into pages, like the models.
shadow-pages.html:
To know what is in shadow, each light renders the scene from its own point of view into a shadow map: a picture of distances. The engine cuts these maps into pages.

  • The sun covers the view with a few maps, fine near the camera and coarser far away.
  • When the camera moves a little, only the strip of pages that came into view is redrawn; the others are kept.
  • A page that is not ready yet borrows the coarser map, so a shadow is never missing.

In depth: docs/SHADOWS.md.

IDENTITY_MATRIX4.description: Column-major identity, read and never written: the pose of a node or of a root with no pose.
values: Sixteen numbers, column-major.

DiagnosticMode.description: What a frame draws. Availability describes real pipeline outputs, never synthetic overlays: `DIAGNOSTICS` gives, per mode, whether the active renderer can produce it and why not.
values: The lit image, from the glTF materials.
The edges of every submitted triangle, lines only, seen through the surfaces.
The edges of every triangle the cut submitted, seen through the surfaces: what the frustum, the detail levels, the HLOD and the occlusion test dropped is absent, what they kept shows even hidden.
A filled unique colour per submitted triangle.
Stable primitive/page identity, one colour per cluster.
Level-0 clusters against the coarser DAG reductions actually selected this frame.
Where each HLOD level starts: white an object near, blue HLOD 0 (its own meshes batched, past the main loading range), then yellow, purple and cyan the coarser levels.
The per-cluster error projected through the cluster sphere, as the cut uses it.
One colour per material class: the class pass that resolved the pixel.
Selected visible pages; rejected hierarchy nodes are counted, not drawn.
Attached index pages; missing pages are not drawn. Not physical VRAM.
Unavailable: texture mip residency is not instrumented.
Unavailable: no fragment counter.
Black: the pixel did not change since the last frame. Grey to white: it changed, eight times amplified — whatever flickers lights up.
Only the light the surfaces reflect, from the screen trace and the probes; black where nothing is reflected.
How much sunlight reaches each surface — white: lit, black: in shadow. No material colour.
All the light on a white surface: direct, reflected, bounced and ambient. No material colour.
The normal image without temporal accumulation: the raw image of this frame, its aliasing and noise included.
The image the temporal AA receives, jitter on, nothing accumulated: each pixel shows the rendered pixel it falls in — it shimmers from frame to frame.
How much history each pixel keeps — white: history kept, black: rejected (a change of shading, off screen).
How much history each pixel holds after the update — white: a full history, black: it starts again. Grey: still converging.
The flicker measure — red: its error, green: how many flickers it counted, blue: the transparents' coverage that cancels it.
The shading rejection, white: history kept — red: without the flicker widening, green: with it, blue: spread to the neighbours, what the update applies.
Why the history restarts — red: disoccluded, green: disoccluded and filled with the occluder's motion, blue: off the last screen.
The motion the accumulation sees — red: moving for the flicker measure, green: a pixel animation, blue: the reprojection edge (white: flat motion).
Thin geometry — red: how far the history clamp relaxes, green: a cluster hole region, blue: the coverage history.
White: a material whose history stays responsive — the accumulation takes a quarter of each new image there.

LodQualityId.description: Runtime LOD presets. `pixelError` is the screen-space threshold the exact-cluster selection consumes; `0` keeps the exact leaves.
values: Maximum source detail — `pixelError: 0`, source anisotropy.
High quality — `pixelError: 1`, maximum anisotropy.
Balanced — `pixelError: 4`.
Adaptive — `pixelError: 2`, raised with camera speed by `adaptivePixelError(base, speed, radius)`; a still view keeps the base.

JobStatus.description: Lifecycle of a job created by `createJob` — a compilation, a world creation. A cancelled or failed job disposes the result it owned.
values: Created, not started.
Running; `progress` events carry a phase and a count.
Resolved; `result` holds the value.
Aborted through its `AbortSignal`.
Threw; `error` holds `{ code, message }`.

CapabilityTier.description: What the safety policy decides a session may run, from measured costs. A `SafetyDecision` carries the tier, whether the feature is enabled, the reason, and when it changed.
values: Every measured cost within budget.
A budget exceeded: the feature is reduced.
The safe path, the feature disabled.

GpuTimingMethod.description: How the GPU durations of a stage profile were taken. A per-pass duration says where, never how much: on a tile-based GPU passes overlap and a pass absorbs its neighbours. The frame total is `gpuImageMs`, the envelope — stage durations do not add into it.
values: Native WebGPU timestamp queries.

ColumnKind.description: Storage of one column of the binary manifest. `COLUMN_KIND` maps each column name to its kind, so a reader knows the view to take over the sidecar bytes.
values: Bounds, spheres, errors, culling nodes.
Signed indices — page integers, group levels.
Unsigned counters and offsets.
Raw bytes — SHA objects, preview pixels.

Side-common.description: Which faces of a surface are drawn — every raster, cone, pipeline and blend-plan decision compares against it. Two readers of `packages/sdk-browser/src/scene/materialSide.ts` stand between it and a host: `sideOf(material: HostMaterials): Side` reads what a host material declares, once at the import boundary, the only place naming the host constants; `materialSide(material: HostMaterials): number` returns that host constant itself, for the diagnostic materials still built with the host library.
values: Front faces only (an empty material array gives this).
Back faces only.
Both, for leaves, fabric and thin cut-outs.

prepare.description: Compiles a source scene into the cache the browser reads. Runs the native compiler — the production path — and returns the manifest read from disk, its `metrics` completed by what only the pointer holds (`wallMs`, `pruneMs`). A source whose product is already in the cache is not recompiled: the folder is proven file by file and kept, and `reused` says what was checked (`null` when the job compiled). `resourceBaseUrl` is required: it is the URL the browser will fetch pages and textures from. What each reader does to its source — polygon faces cut as a fan when convex, by ear clipping otherwise — is in `docs/COMPILER.md`.

prepareMany.description: Prepares many models in one compiler process. The compiler runs `workers` jobs at a time and splits `ramBudgetMb` between them. Resolves with the batch summary — pointers only, nothing read back from disk.

createJob.description: Wraps any pending operation in the engine job contract: a snapshot (`JobStatus`, progress, result, error), subscription, and an abort that disposes what the job owned. The operation must support abort through its owner (RAF, readback, …).

detectCapabilities.description: What this machine's WebGPU actually grants, before a world is created: `{ tier, adapter, extensions, reason }`. The tier is `full` with GPU timestamp queries, `degraded` without them and `unavailable` with no adapter. The reason is always given, so an unsupported capability is reported rather than assumed. The public wrapper a world reads is `capability.detect()` — `{ webgpu, tier, features, reason }`, a simpler shape for the same probe.

perspectiveProjection.description: Perspective projection of a camera with vertical `fov` in degrees, ratio `aspect`, near plane `near`, zoom `zoom`. **Reversed depth, infinite far plane**: `near` projects to 1, infinity to 0. No far plane enters here, hence no division by it — which is what buys the depth precision.

createCameraFrame.description: The matrices of a camera frame, allocated once and rewritten every frame: `view` (the inverse of the camera world matrix), `viewProjection`, and `planes`, the six normalised planes of that frustum.

updateCameraFrame.description: Rewrites the frame: view = the inverse of `world` (zero for a singular world matrix), view-projection = `projection · view`, and the six planes of that frustum. One depth convention crosses all three. `far` is the plane **declared by the host**: the projection has none — it is infinite, which is the whole point of reversed Z — but the frustum keeps it, otherwise a frame would suddenly gain every object the camera was not showing. Omitted or non-finite, the far plane stays unbounded.

worldToRenderOrigin.description: Writes `world` with its translation brought back to `origin`. The subtraction happens in the precision of the inputs — the double of the engine world matrices — and writing a single-precision buffer rounds **after** it, never before: that is all that separates a sharp image from one that shivers. `at` is the rank of the first of the sixteen numbers written, so a buffer of many matrices fills without slicing a view per matrix per frame.

matrixAtRenderOrigin.description: Writes `m · T(origin)`: the same matrix, applied to a point referred to `origin`. Only the fourth column changes, and it equals `m · (origin, 1)`, computed in the precision of the inputs before the write rounding.

viewToRenderOrigin.description: Writes `view` without its translation: the view of a camera of the same orientation posed at the origin of the render frame — the exact counterpart of `worldToRenderOrigin`, the relative world already carrying the eye translation.

createEngineCamera.description: An `EngineCamera`: a camera frame plus `world`, `projection`, `eye`, `near`, `far`, `fov`, `aspect`, every buffer allocated once. This is the engine's own camera — no host object crosses into the runtime.

writeEngineCamera.description: Everything a frame reads, derived from the `into.world` already set and the declared optics.

defaultEngineCamera.description: The camera at the origin with fov 50, aspect 1, near 0.1, far 2000, zoom 1 — the fallback of oracles called before the first frame.

readCameraWorld.description: Resolves the host camera's ancestors, copies its world matrix, then applies `writeEngineCamera`. The only translation from a host camera, once per frame; `HostCamera` is a shape — pose, optics, world matrix, the host's own projection — not a type of the host's rendering library. `aspect` is the ratio the view is drawn at when it is not the one the camera declares: a surface capture renders the same camera aside, at the shape of the surface it writes into. The clip-depth convention is the engine's own, composed from the declared optics in reversed depth with an infinite far plane; nothing of the host's is read here.

holdCameraWorld.description: A bit-for-bit copy of an engine camera, nothing recomputed.

enginePose.description: The position and rotation of the drawn frame, read from the engine camera.

multiplyMatrix4.description: `out = a · b`. The thirty-two inputs are read before the first write, so `out` may be `a` or `b`. Each term is the sum of four products with no initial zero — a sum started at `0` would change the sign of a negative zero. **One buffer type only, `Float64Array`, in and out**: a single caller passing a plain array would make the forty-eight access sites polymorphic and every hot loop would pay it, so a caller starting from a host matrix copies it first.

invertMatrix4.description: `out = m⁻¹` by cofactors. An exactly zero determinant yields the zero matrix — a caller that must distinguish this case tests the determinant, never the output. That threshold is the exact zero, not the engine singularity rule, which applies only where a normal is transported. The sixteen inputs are read before the first write, so `out` may be `m`.

composeMatrix4.description: `out = T · R · S`, the quaternion ordered `(x, y, z, w)`. The last row is written `(0, 0, 0, 1)` exactly; quaternion products are doubled by addition (`x + x`), never multiplied by two.

decomposeMatrix4.description: The reverse: a column's scale is its length, and a negative determinant is carried by the `x` axis alone, whichever axis was reversed at the source. A sheared matrix has no such decomposition — the rotation returned is then that of the column-normalised matrix and recomposition no longer yields `m`, a gap identical to the reference's and quantified by the bench.

copyMatrix4.description: Copies the sixteen numbers of `m` into `out`, each at its offset. A loop rather than `TypedArray.set`: on a view `set` costs a native call, and the outputs are not all typed — a host matrix, a GPU single-precision buffer, which is the only conversion.

determinantMatrix4.description: The 4×4 determinant, expanded along the last row like the reference, and that of the linear part alone (the 3×3 block), expanded along the first column. The sign of the second says whether the transform reverses orientation, hence which face a draw must cull. The second is not the expansion of the first: the relative gap is a few ulps, and the signs can differ only near a singular matrix, where neither rounding decides.

normalMatrix3.description: `out = transpose(inverse(3×3 block of m))` on nine numbers, column-major: the matrix that carries the normals of a surface transformed by `m`, shear and non-uniform scale included. The inverse is the reference one, cofactors and product order included, then transposed with no floating-point operation. **On a singular matrix it writes the adjugate, undivided**, not the reference's zero matrix: a singular pose does not erase a surface, it flattens it onto a plane, and the adjugate applied to a local normal *is* the cross product of the transformed edges, sign included — every consumer then normalises. Only a zero, infinite or NaN scale is written apart, as nine zeros.

linearPartScale.description: The engine's one singularity rule, in the form of the WGSL kernel. The scale is the sum of the absolute values of the nine terms of the linear part; the determinant is taken on the columns **divided by that scale before the product**, never on the raw determinant divided by its cube — `t³` overflows past 1e103 and vanishes under 1e-103, exactly where the rule is meant to decide. `adjugateFactor` then returns `1 / determinant` for a regular matrix (the reference bits), `1` for a singular one (the adjugate as-is), and `null` when the scale is not finite and strictly positive, where the adjugate itself must be replaced by zero.

basisMatrix4.description: The columns `u`, `v`, `n` then the origin, last row `(0, 0, 0, 1)`; and a uniform scale `s` placed at `center`. Both replace a two-call sequence of the host library with one write.

dotVector3.description: `a · b` on three components read at `aAt` and `bAt`: one buffer plus an offset, never a view — that is what makes it cheap inside a loop over thousands of vectors.

crossVector3.description: `out = a × b`. The six components are read before the first write, so `out` may be `a` or `b`.

lengthSqVector3.description: `x² + y² + z²`, the three squares summed in the reference's order. `Math.sqrt` of it is the reference's `length()` bit for bit.

normalizeVector3.description: `v / ‖v‖` in place — each component multiplied by `1 / (length || 1)`, so a zero vector is left unchanged.

scaleVector3.description: The three components multiplied in place; `out = a · s` written at an offset; and `out += a · s`.

transformAffinePoint.description: `M · (x, y, z, 1)` without perspective divide — the form of an affine matrix, whose last row is `(0, 0, 0, 1)`. For such a matrix and a finite point this is bit for bit the projective transform, whose `1 / w` factor is then 1. The coordinates arrive as parameters, so `out` may be the input vector.

transformHomogeneousPoint.description: The four homogeneous components, no divide: the point in clip space when `M` is a view-projection. The caller divides by the fourth, after discarding the one that is zero or non-finite.

transformDirectionVector3.description: The 3×3 block of an affine 4×4 applied to a direction, then the reference normalisation — translation ignored, as for any direction. And `M · (x, y, z)` for a 3×3 matrix stored column-major on nine numbers.

srgbToLinear.description: The exact sRGB curve — `c / 12.92` below 0.04045, `((c + 0.055) / 1.055)^2.4` above — and its inverse, negatives clamped to zero before the exponent.

hslToRgb.description: Hue, saturation and lightness to three RGB components written at `out[o..o+2]`. The reference `setHSL` term by term: wrapped hue, saturation and lightness clamped to `[0, 1]`, zero saturation returned as grey, then the piecewise ramp. The RGB comes out in the encoding the HSL is given in: no transfer curve is applied.

boxUnion.description: A box is six numbers stored flat from `o`: three lower bounds, three upper. An empty box has its lower bounds at `+Infinity` and its upper at `-Infinity`; a NaN bound does not make a box empty. Expanding and uniting take the bounds as parameters, so no temporary object is built per call.

boxTransform.description: The box enclosing the image of `box` by `m`: the union of its eight transformed corners. An empty box stays as is, bounds included, and `out` may be `box` — bounds are read before the first write. `boxCornersInto` writes those eight corners flat, twenty-four numbers: corner `i` takes the upper bound on `x` when bit 1 is set, on `y` for bit 2, on `z` for bit 4, each corner being the homogeneous transform `(m·p) / (m₃·p)`.

sphereFromBounds.description: The bounding sphere of a box, written flat from `o`: centre `x, y, z` then radius. The centre is `(min + max) * 0.5`, the radius half the diagonal. An empty box — an upper bound below its lower — yields the empty sphere, zero centre and radius `-1`. This is the reference box arithmetic term by term, NaN, signed zeros and infinities included.

frustumPlanesFromMatrix.description: The six planes of the frustum of a clip matrix — a view-projection, or a projection alone for planes in view space. The first normalises them, so `a·x + b·y + c·z + d` is a signed distance; the second leaves the raw sums and differences of the rows, where the sign alone decides, with no square root or division: the form of the exact clip test, where normalising would shift the rounding. A degenerate matrix yields NaN or infinite planes without throwing.

frustumFarPlane.description: The far plane of a frustum whose projection has none. The engine projection is infinite: its depth row no longer bounds anything, so the far plane is read from the **view** matrix, whose third row gives the view depth — a point is inside when `far + z >= 0`. A non-finite `far` leaves the zero plane in place, a truly unbounded far plane.

frustumExcludesBox.description: The box against the frustum: the first is true when a plane leaves all eight corners behind. The second returns three states — 0 outside, 1 straddling, 2 entirely inside — in two passes, the first only rejecting, the second reading the most trailing corner to tell "straddling" from "inside". A subtree entirely inside saves a test on every box underneath it.

createTransformTree.description: The engine transform hierarchy, data-oriented: a node is an index into flat arrays — parent, flags, position, quaternion `(x, y, z, w)`, scale, local matrix, world matrix. `localViews[i]` and `worldViews[i]` are sixteen-number views created at growth and never during an update: the GPU reads the whole buffer, a kernel reads a node's view. A fresh node is the reference's fresh object: zero position, identity rotation, scale 1, identity matrices, automatic update. A growth replaces every array, so a caller re-reads `tree.world` or `tree.worldViews` after an add.

setNodePosition.description: Writes go through the setters, which mark what they changed — that mark is what an update reads to decide whom to visit. Under automatic update the next update recomposes the local matrix from the pose, as the reference overwrites `matrix`; `setNodeAutoUpdate(tree, node, false)` keeps the matrix a caller wrote.

reparentTransformNode.description: Attaches `node` under `parent` (`-1`: a root) like the reference `add` — matrices do not move until the next update — and throws if `parent` is `node` or one of its descendants. Removing takes the node and all its descendants, their indices reused afterwards; to detach a subtree while keeping it, reparent it to `-1`.

updateNodeMatrixWorld.description: The node and its whole subtree, parents first. A node is reached if it updates automatically, if it is marked, or if `force`. The stamp of a visited node is `2 · traversal + reached`, so one read tells a child whether it is in the subtree and what its parent passes it. The second form also walks the ancestors from the root, when asked.

lookAtNode.description: Turns `node` toward the world point `(x, y, z)`. `viewer` is true for a camera or a light, which look toward their `−z`, false for an object, which presents its `+z`. `up` is the node's up, `(0, 1, 0)` by default. Ancestors and the node are updated first.

frustumKeepsBoxBatch.description: `n` boxes of six numbers (min then max) against the twenty-four floats of a frustum: `kept[i]` is 1 where the box intersects or sits inside, and the count kept is returned — `frustumExcludesBox` negated, the polarity the reference answers in. The sphere batch writes `SPHERE_VALUES` numbers per box, centre then radius to the corner, as `sphereFromBounds` does. Both loops live in `packages/math/src/batch/culling.ts`.

boxUnionBatch.description: `into` grown by `n` boxes, or by `n` boxes each transformed by its own matrix first — one pass, one scratch box, no allocation. Both repeat `boxUnion`, the second `boxTransform` before it: the world bounds of a whole scene in one call.

invertMatrix4Batch.description: `n` inverses, `n` normal matrices of `NORMAL_MATRIX_VALUES` numbers, `n` compositions `T · R · S`, `n` decompositions. A matrix with a zero determinant is inverted to the identity and flagged in `singular[i]` — never a throw in the middle of a batch. `composeMatrix4Batch` takes everything flat or everything as sub-views, and settles the form before the loop. The four loops live in `packages/math/src/batch/transforms.ts`.

transformPointsBatch.description: `n` points of three numbers by one affine matrix, or one matrix per point; `n` directions by the upper 3×3 then normalised, translation ignored. They repeat `transformAffinePoint` and `transformDirectionVector3`.

srgbToLinearBatch.description: One channel per element, the exact curves of `packages/math/src/color/color.ts`: the reference multiplies by rounded constants, and the gap — invisible at 8 bits — is bounded once, in the bench that duels it.

scene-editor.title: Build a scene with the editor
scene-editor.description: Add shapes and lights, pick them with the mouse, move them with handles, recolour them, save the scene and open it again — in the portal, on the public API alone.
scene-editor.html:
The scene editor is a page of this portal built on three doors of the engine and nothing else. Start from an empty scene: Add → Box, then Add → Directional light. Click the box: world.raycast finds it under the pointer, and the handles of controls.transform appear on it. Drag an arrow to move it — the camera rests while a handle is held — press E to turn it, R to scale it. Change its colour in the inspector: the engine repaints the material in place, the frame's cost stays in the stats corner. Save downloads scene.toJSON; New, then Open, builds the same scene again with scene.fromJSON.

Every step is undone with Ctrl+Z, and the scene is kept in the browser between two visits. Nothing is drawn or moved by the page itself: what you see is the engine.

pick-with-the-pointer.title: Pick an object with the pointer
pick-with-the-pointer.description: `world.raycast` returns the nearest object under a canvas point: the node the page added, the point and normal hit, the distance.
pick-with-the-pointer.html: The test runs on the CPU over the scene's own geometry: triangle meshes triangle by triangle, a loaded model on its box, lines and points never. Hidden subtrees and helper marks are skipped. See it in Click to pick.

move-with-handles.title: Move, turn and scale with handles
move-with-handles.description: `controls.transform(world)` puts handles on one object; a drag writes its pose through its parents, and the camera rests meanwhile.
move-with-handles.html: Modes translate, rotate and scale, world or local axes, optional steps. The events dragStart and dragEnd frame one drag — one undo step. See it in Move, rotate, scale.

save-and-open-a-scene.title: Save and open a scene
save-and-open-a-scene.description: `scene.toJSON(camera)` writes the scene as plain versioned JSON; `scene.fromJSON(json, camera)` builds it again.
save-and-open-a-scene.html: Shapes are stored by the call that built them, materials by their values, loaded models by their address — never inlined — and helper marks not at all. Another format version is refused by name. See it in Save the scene.
